summary: The run developed strong offensive tools and several exhaust/block synergies, but repeatedly paid substantial HP costs and entered Act 2 with little margin for error. The decisive failure was not simply the final turn: earlier damage left the character vulnerable, and the final Collector fight then converted several defensive turns into a rapid collapse from 38 HP to 3 HP. Card choices were broadly functional, but later marginal attacks increased deck size without clearly improving consistency.

lessons.title: Treat HP-loss events as a limited budget
lessons.situation: When an event offers upgrades or rewards for immediate HP loss while the run still has several combats before a safe rest.
lessons.lesson: Do not stack HP-loss events unless the resulting HP remains comfortably survivable; after taking one costly event, prefer preserving HP at the next event rather than paying another fixed loss for a marginal benefit.
evidence_points: Act 1 Floor 4: entered the random-upgrade event at 68/72 HP and chose the option that lost 14 HP, ending at 54/72.
Act 1 Floor 5: at 54/72 HP, chose the removal event and lost another 7 HP, reaching 47/72 before the next combats.
The next two combat summaries ended at 15/72 and 4/72 HP, forcing repeated rests and leaving very little margin for the Guardian sequence.
lessons.reasoning: The individual event choices were not immediately lethal, but their costs compounded with subsequent combat damage. A future run should evaluate the post-event HP against the number of upcoming fights, not just the immediate value of the reward.

lessons.title: At critical HP, compare marginal block with decisive damage
lessons.situation: During a boss fight when HP is already low and the hand contains a high-impact attack alongside several small block cards.
lessons.lesson: Before spending an entire turn on incremental defense, check whether a high-impact attack can remove or substantially weaken the immediate threat; when exact incoming damage is uncertain, treat this as a damage-race hypothesis rather than assuming more block is always correct.
evidence_points: Turn 5 of the Collector fight began at 38/82 HP with 3 energy and Fiend Fire legal, but the chosen sequence was Shrug It Off, True Grit, and Defend, ending the turn without an attack.
The following state showed HP still at 38 but only 6 block before Turn 6, and Turn 6 began at 6/82 HP after the enemy attack.
On Turn 6 at 6/82 HP, Clothesline was played on Torch Head while Collector remained at 175 HP; on Turn 7 the character reached 3/82 HP and ended with Torch Head still alive at 12 HP.
lessons.reasoning: The log does not expose exact incoming damage or prove that Fiend Fire would have been strictly superior, but it does show a defensive sequence followed by a severe HP collapse. In future boss turns, explicitly compare the survival value of available block against the possibility of ending the threatening enemy or advancing the boss damage race.

lessons.title: Stop adding marginal attacks once the core deck is online
lessons.situation: In Act 2, after acquiring a functional damage package and exhaust/block synergies, when the reward alternatives are mediocre attacks.
lessons.lesson: Prefer skipping weak or redundant attacks unless they solve a clear damage breakpoint; preserving a smaller deck is especially valuable when it already contains Fiend Fire, Feel No Pain, Dark Embrace, multiple Shrugs, and other established tools.
evidence_points: Act 2 Floor 25 offered Clash, Perfected Strike, or Iron Wave, and after repeatedly skipping that reward the run ultimately chose Iron Wave.
Act 2 Floor 29 offered Fire Breathing, Intimidate, or Twin Strike, and the run chose Twin Strike.
The final 29-card deck contained Iron Wave, Twin Strike, Anger, two Fiend Fires, and multiple other attacks, alongside the intended exhaust/block engine.
lessons.reasoning: The final deck already had substantial offensive density and useful exhaust synergies, so the later Iron Wave and Twin Strike additions were unlikely to improve consistency as much as retaining a smaller deck would. The reusable rule is to demand a specific role or breakpoint from late Act 2 attack rewards before adding them.
